medical.title: Low vitamin D could be keeping you up at night
medical.summary: Tossing and turning at night? The problem might not be your mattress—it could be your vitamin D levels.

medical.title: How antibody therapy reverses type 1 diabetes in mice
medical.summary: Researchers at UC Davis Health have uncovered key mechanisms behind an experimental antibody that reverses type 1 diabetes (T1D) in mice. Findings from their study, published in the journal Diabetes, could advance efforts to develop treatments for patients with acute T1D.

medical.title: Smarter EHR alerts increase use of first-line antibiotics for patients with penicillin allergy labels
medical.summary: Researchers at Vanderbilt Health successfully redesigned electronic health record (EHR) pop-up alerts that appear when clinicians prescribe antibiotics to patients with penicillin allergies. This adjustment significantly reduced alarm notifications for clinicians and safely provided more patients with first-line antibiotics, cephalosporins, despite their untested penicillin allergies.

medical.title: Biotech firm predicts its antibody injections could compete with COVID vaccines
medical.summary: A biotech company yesterday announced that its lab-grown antibodies may provide an alternative to COVID vaccines.

medical.title: Textile electrodes could bring wearable relief for menstrual pain and muscle soreness
medical.summary: Applying a mild electrical current through the skin is a drug-free way to manage menstrual pain and intense muscle soreness, but at-home devices that deliver the current are bulky and difficult to use effectively, and they require sticky gels. Now, scientists reporting in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces have developed a reusable pain-relieving textile electrode that could be incorporated into clothing. In a preliminary test, the electrodes transmitted electrical stimulation through skin-care products to a person's skin.

medical.title: Growing miniature tumors to help personalize cancer treatment
medical.summary: Modern cancer care is based on many factors. Physicians use scans, lab tests and decades of clinical research to help decide which treatments are best for patients.

medical.title: How persistent inflammation reprograms the immune system to promote T-cell exhaustion
medical.summary: When the body encounters an infection, its immune system must respond rapidly and effectively. Dendritic cells play a central role in this process. They detect pathogens, capture their components and activate specialized immune cells known as CD8 T cells, which can recognize and eliminate infected cells.

medical.title: E-scooter injuries can cause lasting symptoms and work disruption
medical.summary: Many people treated for traumatic brain injury (TBI) after electric scooter crashes experience significant time away from work and symptoms that persist for months, according to findings published Nov. 17 in JAMA Network Open.

medical.title: Cosmetic surgery is on the rise globally. Social media, celebrities reduce taboos and influence beauty ideals
medical.summary: Nearly 18 million cosmetic surgeries were performed worldwide in 2025, increasing by roughly 25% since 2021.

medical.title: Pimple‑popping videos can be disgusting—and strangely satisfying
medical.summary: Some people relax by watching someone squeeze pus from a stranger's face. I'm one of them. I have favorite accounts, strong opinions about technique and very little patience for a video that ends before the pore has been properly cleared.

medical.title: Glucose sensors for type 2 diabetes deserve second look from NHS
medical.summary: A wearable sensor that allows people with type 2 diabetes using insulin to track their glucose levels in real time could prove good value for the NHS, a University of Manchester–led study suggests. The research, published in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, assessed the value for money of real-time continuous glucose monitoring compared with standard finger-prick testing.

medical.title: Researchers look beyond the screen to help keep seniors, people with cognitive concerns connected
medical.summary: Nancy Roderer '73's online physical therapy sessions are an important part of her routine, so she initially brushed off a recent stumble she took while logged on alone at home.

medical.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding bone disease with 'catastrophic' impact on new moms may be missed by doctors
medical.summary: An in-depth study of women with pregnancy and lactation-associated osteoporosis (PLO), a rare condition affecting around 50 women a year in the U.K., found it causes debilitating multiple fractures, acute and chronic pain, disability and long-term psychological distress. The research was carried out by Imperial College London, Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust and the Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital NHS Trust and is published in Osteoporosis International.

medical.title: Paxlovid tied to 12% lower risk of long COVID in high-risk adults
medical.summary: Adults at high risk for severe COVID-19 who were prescribed nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) within five days of infection were less likely to be hospitalized or die in the next six months than those who weren't given the antiviral drug, according to a large study published in PLOS Global Public Health. For patients at low risk for severe outcomes, the results were inconclusive.

medical.title: Flu vaccine might help stave off early signs of Alzheimer's
medical.summary: Brain health is a concern for many older adults because it's tied to their longevity and independence. A new study published in the Annals of Geriatric Medicine and Research finds that getting the flu shot might help people stay sharp, as vaccinated adults were less likely to experience signs of dementia.

medical.title: Researchers develop a novel scaffold HPK1 inhibitor for cancer immunotherapy
medical.summary: Scientists have recently developed IHMT-HPK1-550, a small-molecule HPK1 inhibitor featuring a novel scaffold, providing a new candidate compound for cancer immunotherapy. The study was led by professor Liu Qingsong from the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and the findings were published in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry on Oct. 28.

medical.title: Norovirus is spreading—how to recognize the symptoms and what to do
medical.summary: Described as the "Ferrari of the virus world" for the way it races from person to person, norovirus is once again on the move as we head into winter.

medical.title: Large clinical trial clarifies clot prevention trade-offs after hip and knee replacement
medical.summary: A large, multisite clinical trial involving researchers at the University of Maryland School of Medicine (UMSOM) has provided important new evidence about the medications commonly used to prevent potentially life-threatening blood clots following hip and knee replacement surgery.

medical.title: Blood tests and new cancer models reveal how small cell lung cancer responds to and resists tarlatamab
medical.summary: Researchers at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute have used a blood-based test combined with the development of new preclinical models to follow how small cell lung cancer responds to tarlatamab and changes as it becomes resistant. The study identified a tumor subtype associated with greater treatment benefit and revealed two ways the cancer may escape therapy.

medical.title: Brain lesions: What causes them and when they need follow‑up
medical.summary: You open your brain scan report and see the word "lesion." It's a worrying word to come across while waiting to speak to your doctor. In a report, it means there's an area in or around the brain that looks abnormal on the scan. That could be anything from an area of tissue damaged by a stroke to a pocket of fluid that's been there for years.

medical.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
medical.summary: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.

medical.title: Why don't weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy work for everyone?
medical.summary: Why do Ozempic and Wegovy produce dramatic weight loss for some people but disappointing results for others? Scientists are investigating whether the body's hidden energy-saving response could help explain the difference and unlock more effective, personalized weight-loss treatments.

medical.title: Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer
medical.summary: Scientists have discovered a rare inherited mutation in the CDK12 gene linked to aggressive prostate cancer, with all five identified carriers developing metastatic disease between ages 44 and 62. The finding could lead to expanded genetic testing, helping families uncover hidden cancer risks and potentially detect the disease while it is still treatable.

medical.title: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive
medical.summary: Exercising too much without adequate recovery may disrupt brain chemistry in surprising ways. Scientists found that mice subjected to prolonged, intense training had elevated dopamine levels in a brain region linked to memory and emotions, even 48 hours after exercising. The discovery could help explain why overtrained athletes sometimes struggle with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue, although these symptoms were not directly measured.

medical.title: Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut
medical.summary: The secret behind truly terrible-smelling farts lies in tiny amounts of sulfur-containing gases produced by gut bacteria as they digest food. Scientists reveal why some foods make farts smell worse, why loud farts aren't always the stinkiest, and how our noses evolved to detect these powerful odors.

science.title: Researchers reveal inner-core structural evolution of Typhoon Bavi using multisensor satellite observations
science.summary: Tropical cyclones frequently undergo rapid, complex structural changes within their inner cores, such as eyewall replacement and wind-field expansion, that strongly influence typhoon intensity and coastal hazards. However, capturing these multilayered transformations continuously from the ocean surface to the upper cloud tops remains a major observational challenge.

science.title: DNA at nuclear edges forms protective UV shield in developing roundworm embryos
science.summary: Inside the cell nucleus, DNA is arranged into neighborhoods, some of which are tightly packed and mostly inactive. This so-called heterochromatin typically associates with the nuclear lamina, a meshwork lining the inside of the nuclear envelope. This arrangement helps organize the genome and regulate gene activity. But how and when it forms during embryonic development has remained unclear.

science.title: NASA+ Content Coming to Big Screen at Greenbelt, Maryland Cinema
science.summary: NASA announced Monday that NASA+ content has found its first theatrical home at The Greenbelt Cinema in Greenbelt, Maryland, expanding the agency’s reach across major viewing platforms and bringing space even closer to home. “The National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958 calls us to share our story of space exploration with the broadest possible […]

science.title: A common language for pistachio growth: Researchers develop a crop-monitoring scale
science.summary: The pistachio BBCH scale, created by the University of Córdoba, standardizes phenological monitoring of the crop, enabling researchers and farmers to identify its growth stage quickly and easily.

science.title: Flexible simulations model how dark matter collisions may leave their fingerprints on the universe
science.summary: We cannot see or measure dark matter directly. Yet scientists are convinced that it exists and that it accounts for around 85% of all matter in the universe, including the matter that everything here on Earth is made of, from earthworms and mountains to seawater and washing machines.

science.title: Teams Lock in Mission Architecture for NASA’s SR-1 Freedom
science.summary: NASA completed a major review for Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom and locked in key elements of the spacecraft, which is targeted to launch in 2028 and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space for the first time.   Experts from across the agency, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), and industry met at NASA’s Glenn Research […]

science.title: Evolution keeps returning to simple leaves
science.summary: A study led by researchers from the University of Oxford has explained a long-standing riddle: why do most plants have leaves with a very simple shape? In a new study published Nov. 24, they explain why complex leaves have evolved again and again—only for evolution to repeatedly revert to simpler forms.

science.title: Vaporized rock reveals titanium oxide around massive young star for first time
science.summary: Scientists have observed titanium oxide in gas form around a massive, young star for the first time. The finding identifies the first region in which scientists have been able to determine the composition of solid materials outside of our solar system without having to collect a sample and bring it back to Earth.

science.title: Body-positive imagery in ads resonates differently with men and women, study finds
science.summary: Advocates of body-positive advertising, which showcases models who do not fit the traditional molds of thin or muscular models, say they are challenging female beauty standards by rejecting an unhealthy obsession with often unattainable idealized bodies. However, a new Concordia study shows that while women generally respond positively to large-size models, body-positive advertising images are not as effective with men.

science.title: Visible light powers new catalyst to turn carbon dioxide into industrial raw material
science.summary: Rice University researchers have demonstrated a way to split carbon dioxide using visible light without external heating, overcoming a major energy obstacle in sustainable chemical manufacturing.

science.title: California raised minimum wages for fast‑food workers—here's how it played out 2 years later
science.summary: Even before the 2026 midterm elections delivered a clear message about cost-of-living concerns, many states had been raising their minimum wage on their own as one way to increase workers' purchasing power. And some have taken a more targeted approach, setting wage floors for specific industries.

science.title: Planktonic hyperiidean amphipod confirmed in the Aegean Sea, and a new study shows how to identify subadult males
science.summary: Amphipods change in size and shape each time they molt. When a species is told apart from its relatives by small anatomical details, this creates a practical problem: a trait that identifies an adult may be absent or different in the younger animal. A recently published study in Biodiversity Data Journal tests this problem on Phronima atlantica, a planktonic amphipod of the open ocean, and identifies which of its features stay reliable in males from the subadult to the adult stage.

science.title: Brighter signals, cheaper tests: Researchers team up to bring lab-grade detection to smartphones
science.summary: Researchers within The Grainger College of Engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and the Indian Institute of Technology, Kharagpur, are combining two kinds of photonic crystals with new nanoparticles. They want to make fluorescence-based tests sensitive enough to count single molecules, using cameras as cheap as the ones in a smartphone.

science.title: Panic buying? Gradual stockpiling makes for better 'prepping' without emptying supermarket shelves
science.summary: Soon after the government launched its "Be Ready" campaign, supermarket shelves were empty where the bottled water usually sits. Flashlights quickly went out of stock too.

science.title: Copper aluminum oxide could make light-controlling components for smart glasses 120 times thinner
science.summary: Could augmented reality (AR) glasses become as thin and lightweight as everyday eyeglasses? Researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) and their collaborators have identified a material that could reduce the thickness of polarization-control components to approximately 1/120 that of conventional components while maintaining high light transmission. environment.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution

mix_items.summary: Applying a mild electrical current through the skin is a drug-free way to manage menstrual pain and intense muscle soreness, but at-home devices that deliver the current are bulky and difficult to use effectively, and they require sticky gels. Now, scientists reporting in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces have developed a reusable pain-relieving textile electrode that could be incorporated into clothing. In a preliminary test, the electrodes transmitted electrical stimulation through skin-care products to a person's skin.

mix_items.title: Growing miniature tumors to help personalize cancer treatment
mix_items.summary: Modern cancer care is based on many factors. Physicians use scans, lab tests and decades of clinical research to help decide which treatments are best for patients.

mix_items.title: Vaporized rock reveals titanium oxide around massive young star for first time
mix_items.summary: Scientists have observed titanium oxide in gas form around a massive, young star for the first time. The finding identifies the first region in which scientists have been able to determine the composition of solid materials outside of our solar system without having to collect a sample and bring it back to Earth.

mix_items.title: How persistent inflammation reprograms the immune system to promote T-cell exhaustion
mix_items.summary: When the body encounters an infection, its immune system must respond rapidly and effectively. Dendritic cells play a central role in this process. They detect pathogens, capture their components and activate specialized immune cells known as CD8 T cells, which can recognize and eliminate infected cells.

mix_items.title: Body-positive imagery in ads resonates differently with men and women, study finds
mix_items.summary: Advocates of body-positive advertising, which showcases models who do not fit the traditional molds of thin or muscular models, say they are challenging female beauty standards by rejecting an unhealthy obsession with often unattainable idealized bodies. However, a new Concordia study shows that while women generally respond positively to large-size models, body-positive advertising images are not as effective with men.

mix_items.title: Visible light powers new catalyst to turn carbon dioxide into industrial raw material
mix_items.summary: Rice University researchers have demonstrated a way to split carbon dioxide using visible light without external heating, overcoming a major energy obstacle in sustainable chemical manufacturing.

mix_items.title: E-scooter injuries can cause lasting symptoms and work disruption
mix_items.summary: Many people treated for traumatic brain injury (TBI) after electric scooter crashes experience significant time away from work and symptoms that persist for months, according to findings published Nov. 17 in JAMA Network Open.

mix_items.title: California raised minimum wages for fast‑food workers—here's how it played out 2 years later
mix_items.summary: Even before the 2026 midterm elections delivered a clear message about cost-of-living concerns, many states had been raising their minimum wage on their own as one way to increase workers' purchasing power. And some have taken a more targeted approach, setting wage floors for specific industries.

mix_items.title: Cosmetic surgery is on the rise globally. Social media, celebrities reduce taboos and influence beauty ideals
mix_items.summary: Nearly 18 million cosmetic surgeries were performed worldwide in 2025, increasing by roughly 25% since 2021.

mix_items.title: Planktonic hyperiidean amphipod confirmed in the Aegean Sea, and a new study shows how to identify subadult males
mix_items.summary: Amphipods change in size and shape each time they molt. When a species is told apart from its relatives by small anatomical details, this creates a practical problem: a trait that identifies an adult may be absent or different in the younger animal. A recently published study in Biodiversity Data Journal tests this problem on Phronima atlantica, a planktonic amphipod of the open ocean, and identifies which of its features stay reliable in males from the subadult to the adult stage.

mix_items.title: Brighter signals, cheaper tests: Researchers team up to bring lab-grade detection to smartphones
mix_items.summary: Researchers within The Grainger College of Engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and the Indian Institute of Technology, Kharagpur, are combining two kinds of photonic crystals with new nanoparticles. They want to make fluorescence-based tests sensitive enough to count single molecules, using cameras as cheap as the ones in a smartphone.

mix_items.title: ‘We don’t want it’: First Nations reject plan to release mining waste into water source
mix_items.summary: Suncor, Canada’s second-largest oil company, wants to release treated wastewater from mining oil in Alberta’s tar sands into a drinking water source for the community of Fort Chipewyan. Investigative reporter Leana Hosea visited the community to learn more. She joins the Mongabay Newscast this week to detail what she found. “This story is not about […]

mix_items.title: Panic buying? Gradual stockpiling makes for better 'prepping' without emptying supermarket shelves
mix_items.summary: Soon after the government launched its "Be Ready" campaign, supermarket shelves were empty where the bottled water usually sits. Flashlights quickly went out of stock too.

mix_items.title: Pimple‑popping videos can be disgusting—and strangely satisfying
mix_items.summary: Some people relax by watching someone squeeze pus from a stranger's face. I'm one of them. I have favorite accounts, strong opinions about technique and very little patience for a video that ends before the pore has been properly cleared.

mix_items.title: Copper aluminum oxide could make light-controlling components for smart glasses 120 times thinner
mix_items.summary: Could augmented reality (AR) glasses become as thin and lightweight as everyday eyeglasses? Researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) and their collaborators have identified a material that could reduce the thickness of polarization-control components to approximately 1/120 that of conventional components while maintaining high light transmission. The discovery could pave the way for smaller, lighter AR devices and more compact optical communication equipment.

mix_items.title: What is resilience? It may be less about bouncing back than we think
mix_items.summary: Resilience can sound empowering. Yet it can also become a responsibility, a socially imposed burden that people are expected to demonstrate when they are ill, aging or struggling.

mix_items.title: Glucose sensors for type 2 diabetes deserve second look from NHS
mix_items.summary: A wearable sensor that allows people with type 2 diabetes using insulin to track their glucose levels in real time could prove good value for the NHS, a University of Manchester–led study suggests. The research, published in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, assessed the value for money of real-time continuous glucose monitoring compared with standard finger-prick testing.

mix_items.title: DebunkBot can quash emerging conspiracy theories
mix_items.summary: Rumors immediately began circulating after Donald Trump, then a presidential candidate, survived an assassination attempt during an open-air rally on July 13, 2024. Some suspected the "deep state" was responsible, while others thought it was a false flag operation to get Trump reelected.

mix_items.title: NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Mission Overview
mix_items.summary: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. The mission will be the third flight of the company’s Cygnus XL, the larger, more cargo-capable version of the company’s solar-powered spacecraft. The Cygnus XL will launch aboard a […]

mix_items.title: Highly sociable Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins with predictable group size preferences may live longer
mix_items.summary: Aging can bring changes in sociability, such as decreased network size, increased social selectivity, reduced social influence and connectedness and reduced affiliative interactions. A study published Nov. 24 in the open-access journal PLOS Biology by Kelley Caroline Meehan at The University of Queensland, St. Lucia, Australia, and colleagues suggests a relationship in Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins between sociability (group size), its predictability and longevity.

mix_items.title: Effort can deepen understanding without making learning more enjoyable, study suggests
mix_items.summary: As children, many of us resisted being told that studying harder would make learning enjoyable, especially when struggling with math homework. Yet as adults, we may give children the same advice. But does effort really lead to interest, or is it the other way around?

mix_items.title: Researchers look beyond the screen to help keep seniors, people with cognitive concerns connected
mix_items.summary: Nancy Roderer '73's online physical therapy sessions are an important part of her routine, so she initially brushed off a recent stumble she took while logged on alone at home.

mix_items.title: How a feminist lens is shaping my climate reporting (commentary)
mix_items.summary: In university, I took a unit called Environmental Journalism, taught by one of my favorite lecturers. I paid enough attention to pass, but certainly not enough to imagine it becoming a beat I would want to report on. I could not picture myself willingly sifting through scientific research papers, trying to understand ribosomes or learning […]

mix_items.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding bone disease with 'catastrophic' impact on new moms may be missed by doctors
mix_items.summary: An in-depth study of women with pregnancy and lactation-associated osteoporosis (PLO), a rare condition affecting around 50 women a year in the U.K., found it causes debilitating multiple fractures, acute and chronic pain, disability and long-term psychological distress. The research was carried out by Imperial College London, Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust and the Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital NHS Trust and is published in Osteoporosis International.

mix_items.title: Selective logging can better preserve subtropical forest adaptive capacity than clear-cutting
mix_items.summary: Adaptive capacity—the ability to cope with disturbances and environmental change—offers a useful perspective for sustainable forest management. However, applying this concept to logging remains challenging, and a key question is how different logging practices affect forest adaptive capacity.

mix_items.title: Biologists sort bacteria-killing peptides by speed: Slow is smooth, smooth is more effective
mix_items.summary: A quick kill is not always best when battling bacterial infections. Sometimes, as new Stanford research shows, slower is better.

mix_items.title: Paxlovid tied to 12% lower risk of long COVID in high-risk adults
mix_items.summary: Adults at high risk for severe COVID-19 who were prescribed nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) within five days of infection were less likely to be hospitalized or die in the next six months than those who weren't given the antiviral drug, according to a large study published in PLOS Global Public Health. For patients at low risk for severe outcomes, the results were inconclusive.

mix_items.title: Birds respond more quickly to predators in habitats with greater species diversity
mix_items.summary: The diversity of species in a habitat is a common focus of conservation efforts. Local biodiversity has been shown to influence important ecosystem functions like pollination and pest control. In this study, Kumar and colleagues investigated the impact of diversity on the flow of ecological information in the form of defensive bird calls.

mix_items.title: New system enables highly sensitive detection of trace hydrogen
mix_items.summary: A research team led by professor Fang Yonghua at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has developed a new system for detecting trace amounts of hydrogen that improves detection sensitivity by reducing background interference, enabling it to directly detect hydrogen at a concentration of one part per million (ppm).

mix_items.title: Flu vaccine might help stave off early signs of Alzheimer's
mix_items.summary: Brain health is a concern for many older adults because it's tied to their longevity and independence. A new study published in the Annals of Geriatric Medicine and Research finds that getting the flu shot might help people stay sharp, as vaccinated adults were less likely to experience signs of dementia.

mix_items.title: Clouded tiger cats are notoriously hard to catch. This young researcher caught seven
mix_items.summary: Tadeu de Oliveira, founder and leader of the Tiger Cats Conservation Initiative, a group of scientists committed to studying the smallest wildcats of South and Central America, wanted to be crystal clear: “It is rare to catch a tiger cat. Period. Period!” he emphasized in a phone interview from Brazil with Mongabay. “You may ask […]

mix_items.title: Researchers develop a novel scaffold HPK1 inhibitor for cancer immunotherapy
mix_items.summary: Scientists have recently developed IHMT-HPK1-550, a small-molecule HPK1 inhibitor featuring a novel scaffold, providing a new candidate compound for cancer immunotherapy. The study was led by professor Liu Qingsong from the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and the findings were published in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry on Oct. 28.

mix_items.title: Ecuador’s bioeconomy plan vows sustainability, but faces a test of government priorities
mix_items.summary: The government of Ecuador has approved a new 10-year plan to promote economic activities that make use of the country’s biological resources, while also taking steps to conserve the ecosystems that they rely on. It aims to innovate agribusiness, ecotourism, and other industries in rural areas, without threatening the environment or Indigenous communities. The National […]

mix_items.title: Norovirus is spreading—how to recognize the symptoms and what to do
mix_items.summary: Described as the "Ferrari of the virus world" for the way it races from person to person, norovirus is once again on the move as we head into winter.

mix_items.title: Large clinical trial clarifies clot prevention trade-offs after hip and knee replacement
mix_items.summary: A large, multisite clinical trial involving researchers at the University of Maryland School of Medicine (UMSOM) has provided important new evidence about the medications commonly used to prevent potentially life-threatening blood clots following hip and knee replacement surgery.

mix_items.title: Blood tests and new cancer models reveal how small cell lung cancer responds to and resists tarlatamab
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute have used a blood-based test combined with the development of new preclinical models to follow how small cell lung cancer responds to tarlatamab and changes as it becomes resistant. The study identified a tumor subtype associated with greater treatment benefit and revealed two ways the cancer may escape therapy.

mix_items.title: Brain lesions: What causes them and when they need follow‑up
mix_items.summary: You open your brain scan report and see the word "lesion." It's a worrying word to come across while waiting to speak to your doctor. In a report, it means there's an area in or around the brain that looks abnormal on the scan. That could be anything from an area of tissue damaged by a stroke to a pocket of fluid that's been there for years.

mix_items.title: As new season starts, Antarctic krill-fishing vessels face urgent conservation decision (commentary)
mix_items.summary: Despite promising developments, the 27 member states of the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) have again failed to reach an agreement that protects the Southern Ocean. Mired by consensus decision-making and shrouded from public view by confidentiality rules, Antarctica’s governance systems are no longer fulfilling their mandate. This leaves room […]

mix_items.title: In the Bolivian Andes, Indigenous women plant native trees to restore water sources
mix_items.summary: The bare ridges of the Tunari mountain range rise high in Bolivia’s central Cochabamba department. Only the occasional stand of squat, shrubby trees and rust-red potato crops dot the slopes. It wasn’t always this way. The high-elevation landscape was once filled with native Kewiña (Polylepis sp.) trees, a slow-growing tree belonging to the rose family […]

mix_items.title: Indigenous peoples leave collapsed climate talks with promises on hold
mix_items.summary: ANATALYA, Türkiye — A year ago, a record number of Indigenous people attended the United Nations climate summit in Belém, Brazil. Although there as observers, without a seat at the negotiating table, they left with promises: recognition of their lands, a share of a new forest fund, and a just transition mechanism in the making. […]

mix_items.title: Global marine conservation gathering seeks solutions amid mounting ocean challenges
mix_items.summary: EDINBURGH — Ocean conservation efforts are being hindered by inadequate funding, as well as difficulties translating research into action, according to attendees of an international marine conservation congress in Scotland. Between Nov. 13 and 16, nearly 800 attendees from more than 65 countries convened in the Scottish capital, Edinburgh, for the eighth International Marine Conservation […]

mix_items.title: Indonesia fires test palm oil certification scheme as NGOs question RSPO accountability
mix_items.summary: JAKARTA — Environmental groups are questioning the effectiveness of a global organization that develops standards and certification for sustainable palm oil production after fires affected thousands of hectares in concessions belonging to its members in Indonesia — including areas certified under its sustainability scheme. The criticism came as the organization, the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm […]

mix_items.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
mix_items.summary: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.

mix_items.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
mix_items.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

mix_items.title: Why don't weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy work for everyone?
mix_items.summary: Why do Ozempic and Wegovy produce dramatic weight loss for some people but disappointing results for others? Scientists are investigating whether the body's hidden energy-saving response could help explain the difference and unlock more effective, personalized weight-loss treatments.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a rare inherited mutation in the CDK12 gene linked to aggressive prostate cancer, with all five identified carriers developing metastatic disease between ages 44 and 62. The finding could lead to expanded genetic testing, helping families uncover hidden cancer risks and potentially detect the disease while it is still treatable.

mix_items.title: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive
mix_items.summary: Exercising too much without adequate recovery may disrupt brain chemistry in surprising ways. Scientists found that mice subjected to prolonged, intense training had elevated dopamine levels in a brain region linked to memory and emotions, even 48 hours after exercising. The discovery could help explain why overtrained athletes sometimes struggle with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue, although these symptoms were not directly measured.

mix_items.title: Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut
mix_items.summary: The secret behind truly terrible-smelling farts lies in tiny amounts of sulfur-containing gases produced by gut bacteria as they digest food. Scientists reveal why some foods make farts smell worse, why loud farts aren't always the stinkiest, and how our noses evolved to detect these powerful odors.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
mix_items.summary: Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

mix_items.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
mix_items.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

mix_items.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

mix_items.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
mix_items.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.
